# Penny (envelope-os) — Project ISA

> Surface name **Penny**. Codebase folder `envelope-os`. Zero-based envelope budgeting layer on top of PocketSmith, feeding PAI Pulse. AUD, personal-finance-grade security. **Local-first now, cloud-ready by construction.** One codebase ships to two deployment targets — Local (Tailscale, single principal at runtime) and Cloud (public at `nicholaswood.com.au/budget`, multi-tenant) — and the only difference between them is configuration plus two swapped adapters, never the data model or the business logic.

## Problem

PocketSmith owns Nick's bank feeds and categorisation across ANZ (primary), NAB (credit card), and Macquarie, but its envelope handling is weak and it does not implement zero-based envelope budgeting. Dave Ramsey's EveryDollar and similar apps do implement the methodology but cannot connect to Australian banks. The result is that Nick runs envelope budgeting in his head on top of PocketSmith, which does not scale, does not survive a credit-card statement cycle cleanly, and gives no trustworthy single number for "where am I against budget right now". There is no time-travel view of envelope balances at a past date, no enforced every-dollar-allocated discipline, and no surface that feeds the state into Pulse. Secondly, the original build was scoped local-only and single-user; if it works, Nick wants the option to let another person use it by handing over only their email and their own PocketSmith developer key, which a local-only, single-tenant design cannot do without a painful retrofit.

## Vision

Nick opens Pulse and sees one honest line. Unallocated dollars, the worst three overspends, and whether the credit-card holding balance still matches NAB. He opens Penny on his phone — installed as a PWA, reached over Tailscale. He never plans a month; the budget is the recurring template and it simply rolls into each new month on its own. When something changes he adjusts one envelope or moves money, the change is remembered going forward, and it lands in a budget history he can scroll back through. When a late transaction lands weeks later, the envelope it belongs to moves on the day it was spent, not when the statement closes, so the budget never lies about the past. The euphoric surprise is twofold: the holding-versus-NAB tripwire — a single number that, when it drifts, tells Nick something is wrong before he would otherwise have noticed — and the realisation that the day he decides to let someone else use Penny, it is already a per-user multi-tenant app; he adds them with an email and their dev key, flips one config value, deploys to GCP, and nothing in the ledger, the envelope engine, or the UI had to change.

## Out of Scope

The MVP does not split one category across multiple envelopes. Mapping stays many categories to one envelope. A dedicated sinking-fund target type is not built. Annual envelopes are treated as monthly target divided by twelve for the MVP. There is no mobile quick-add of purchases and no offline transaction capture — the PWA is read-and-allocate over Tailscale, not an offline write queue. There is no auto-allocation engine and no agent-proposed allocations. There is no reporting suite beyond what the grid and detail pages show, no PDF or CSV export, and no what-if replay queries against the event log. There is no multi-currency support. There is no joint-finance surface; the data model is multi-tenant per-user, not joint-account shared-ledger. **Cloud hosting is built-ready, not deployed.** The cloud adapters (email magic-link auth, KMS-encrypted per-user secrets, Postgres data layer) are written and unit-tested behind their interfaces so the switch is config-only, but standing up the public GCP service, registering the `/budget` route on `nicholaswood.com.au`, and onboarding a second human are deliberate later steps, not MVP deliverables. Direct bank-CSV reconciliation against PocketSmith feeds is a later trust layer, not MVP.

## Principles

- The envelope is the user-facing primitive. PocketSmith categories are inputs. Envelopes are how Nick thinks and decides.
- Cash-basis fidelity to the envelope metaphor. A swipe decrements the envelope on the day it happens, regardless of which card moved.
- Every dollar is conserved. A forgiven overspend is not free money. The deficit is always booked somewhere, never silently leaked.
- Local-first. Personal financial data does not leave the owner's machine without a deliberate, per-action choice. In local mode there is no cloud egress of transactions at all.
- **Cloud-ready by construction, not by rewrite.** The data model is multi-tenant from the first migration; every piece of identity-bearing state carries a `user_id`. Deployment differences (who authenticates, where secrets live, which database backs the store) sit behind interfaces. Business logic never knows or branches on which deployment target it is running in.
- **One tenant per principal.** Each user owns their own PocketSmith developer key, their own transactions, their own envelopes and budget. There is no shared data between tenants. Onboarding a person is: their email plus their PocketSmith dev key.
- The event log is the source of truth and the audit log. Future-Nick can always ask why an envelope went negative on a given day and get an answer.
- The thing is the source of truth, not the task. This ISA at the project root is iterated continuously, not recreated per task.

## Constraints

- bun plus TypeScript only. No Python. No npm or npx. Australian English. AUD only. No em dashes in prose.
- **Single codebase, two deployment targets, one switch.** A `DEPLOY_MODE` value of `local` or `cloud` is the only thing that selects deployment behaviour. No business module reads `DEPLOY_MODE`; only the composition root (dependency wiring) does.
- **Multi-tenant schema from the first migration.** A `users` table exists. Every tenant-scoped table carries a non-null `user_id` foreign key to `users.id`. Local mode seeds exactly one user (Nick) and runs single-tenant at runtime over a multi-tenant schema. There is no separate single-tenant schema that later needs migrating.
- **Auth sits behind an `AuthProvider` interface.** Local implementation: Tailscale device trust plus a PIN held in the secret store, thirty-minute idle session. Cloud implementation: passwordless email magic-link sign-in (request link, verify token, mint httpOnly+Secure+SameSite session cookie). No route handler or business module depends on which implementation is active; they depend only on the resolved authenticated `user_id`.
- **Secrets sit behind a `SecretStore` interface, keyed per user.** Each user's PocketSmith `X-Developer-Key` is fetched through the store for the authenticated `user_id` at request time. Local implementation: the PAI secrets store / OS keychain / an encrypted local file. Cloud implementation: envelope encryption via GCP KMS with ciphertext stored in the database. A developer key never appears in env files, git, logs, or as plaintext at rest.
- **Data access sits behind a thin store layer; SQL stays Postgres-portable.** Local persistence is SQLite via `bun:sqlite`, single file, single writer owned by one Bun process. No business module imports `bun:sqlite` directly — they depend on the store interface. Business queries avoid SQLite-only syntax so the Postgres adapter (cloud) is a drop-in. The cloud Postgres adapter is written and unit-tested but not the local default.
- The PocketSmith client is generated from the published OpenAPI 3 spec `openapi.json` at `github.com/pocketsmith/api`, pinned to commit SHA `8e964ca0107444e4d797b75fbc30fb969d488d9d` in-repo. The client is regenerated manually on a spec bump, never auto-tracked. Base URL `https://api.pocketsmith.com/v2`. Auth is the `X-Developer-Key` header (not OAuth) in local and cloud alike — the key is the per-user secret.
- Sync is daily pull only. PocketSmith publishes no webhooks, so no push or listener code path may exist. Incremental sync uses `updated_since`.
- **The UI is a PWA, optimised for web app and installed app alike.** It ships a web manifest and a service worker, is installable on iOS and Android home screens, and serves an offline app shell. It is served over HTTPS in both modes: locally via `tailscale serve` on a `*.ts.net` hostname (a real cert, so service workers register and install works); in cloud via the platform certificate at `nicholaswood.com.au/budget`. Remote access in local mode is Tailscale-only; no public internet exposure in local mode.
- No cloud SaaS storage of financial data and no cloud AI inference over transactions in local mode. In cloud mode, financial data is stored in the user's own tenant rows and protected per the security ISCs; cloud AI inference over transactions stays off by default and opt-in per query.

## Goal

Ship a local-first Penny that replaces Nick's PocketSmith-plus-mental-model setup with a real zero-based envelope view, built on a multi-tenant, adapter-seamed architecture that becomes a public per-user cloud app by changing configuration rather than code. Done means: a daily PocketSmith pull lands transactions into a SQLite event-sourced ledger scoped to the authenticated user; envelopes decrement on spend-date with a visible Credit Card Holding envelope for NAB; the recurring budget template auto-rolls into each new month with no manual ritual, a continuous zero-based check alerts when the budget is unbalanced rather than blocking, and actual-versus-budget income variance is carried as surplus/deficit on per-source income envelopes; the grid and a time-travel view render envelope balances; the app runs as an installable PWA reachable over Tailscale HTTPS; a read-only Pulse widget surfaces unallocated dollars, top overspends, and the holding-versus-NAB tripwire; and the cloud-ready seams (multi-tenant schema, `AuthProvider`, `SecretStore`, portable store layer, `DEPLOY_MODE` switch) are in place and unit-tested such that the cloud adapters compile and pass their tests without any business-logic change.

### Ingest and sync (Weekend 1)

### Envelope semantics (Weekend 2)

- [ ] ISC-18: Envelope CRUD persists name, parent_id, group, rollover_rule, target_type, target_amount

## Changelog

- conjectured: LOAD-3 as originally written said default rollover rolls positive, zeroes negative, and carries the negative as visible debt with no auto-true-up.
  refuted_by: Those are two different rules. Zeroing a negative and carrying it as debt cannot both hold. Under zero-based budgeting a forgiven overspend is not free, so the deficit must be booked somewhere or the ledger leaks and the holding tripwire loses meaning.
  learned: The YNAB resolution is correct here. Default zeroes the envelope by booking the deficit into next period available-to-allocate, surfaced as a visible line in the wizard. Standing per-envelope debt is the roll_all override only.
  criterion_now: ISC-25, ISC-26, ISC-28.

  refuted_by: With expected-versus-actual income (NEW-2) a hard per-save block fights reality. Mid-month edits, late actuals, and partial wizard sessions would all be blocked, and viewing must never be blocked.
  learned: Enforce the every-dollar rule at wizard completion against expected income, not on every intermediate save. Divergence of actual from expected is shown as a dashboard delta and prompts re-allocation, never blocks viewing.
  criterion_now: ISC-30, ISC-31, ISC-32.

A dormant column does not deliver that; tenant scoping has to be threaded through every read and write, auth has to resolve a user, and each user's dev key has to be isolated secret material. Retrofitting that into an event-sourced single-principal ledger after the fact is the exact painful migration the architect review warned against.
  learned: Build multi-tenant from migration one and run single-tenant locally. Promote `owner` to a real `users` table with `user_id` on every tenant table, scope every store query by the authenticated user, put auth and secrets behind interfaces, and make deployment a one-switch config.   refuted_by: Nick (2026-06-26): zero-based applies to the budget (the plan), not to actual cash flow. A non-zero-based budget should raise an alert, never block. And income variance should not live on a dashboard line; income is itself an envelope per source, and actual differing from budgeted is a surplus/deficit on that income envelope.
  learned: Two separable rules. (1) The zero-based check compares total spending allocations to total budgeted income and raises an alert on imbalance; saving and viewing are never blocked. (2) Income envelopes are first-class, one per source, each holding a budgeted amount and an actual balance; the variance is the surplus/deficit. This keeps the envelope metaphor whole on the income side and removes the only hard wall the design still had.
  criterion_now: ISC-30, ISC-31, ISC-32, ISC-65.

  refuted_by: Nick (2026-06-26): a reallocation must say where the money comes from and whether the change is one-off or ongoing. Extra income parked in Savings could be a one-time move of this month's surplus, or a permanent decision to expect more income and save more every month. Editing a single number cannot express either the source or the recurrence.
  learned: A reallocation is a move with three parts: destination, named source, and scope (this-month-only vs ongoing). The named source keeps the plan zero-based by construction. There is a recurring budget template behind the months; an ongoing change edits the template (so apply-last-month carries it forward), a this-month change is a period override that leaves the template untouched.   refuted_by: Nick (2026-06-26): any envelope in surplus or deficit should either be balanced by a move (either direction) or carry over, and the carryover must be shown explicitly per envelope. Silently zeroing an envelope and docking a pooled number hides the deficit; Nick wants it visible on the envelope it belongs to.
  learned: Carryover in both directions is the default, shown as an explicit starting-carryover figure on every envelope row. Each envelope row shows four figures: starting carryover, this-period allocation, total available (carryover + allocation), and left (total - spent). The deficit is still conserved (it is the negative carryover, not a leak), so ISC-28 holds. The Edit Budget wizard, not an inline baseline edit, is where the recurring template is changed.

# Basiq Migration Spec — Direct Australian Bank Feeds for Penny (envelope-os)

> Status: DESIGN (pre-build). Authored 2026-06-29. Owns the design for replacing the
> PocketSmith ingest dependency with direct Australian bank feeds via Basiq (CDR /
> Open Banking). The ISCs live in the project ISA (`ISA.md`, ISC-105..ISC-128); this
> document is the detailed design behind those criteria. Basiq API field names and
> sign conventions marked **[confirm-in-sandbox]** must be verified against the live
> Basiq sandbox during BUILD before the matching ISC can pass.

## 1. Why

Three drivers, in Nick's words: drop a dependency, kill the PocketSmith subscription
cost, and stop building on a product that is essentially just a bridge if Penny might
serve other people later.

The decisive structural fact: **Penny is already multi-tenant.** Every `Store` method is
scoped by `userId` (`src/platform/store.ts`), the schema is multi-tenant from migration
one (ISC-47, ISC-48), and cloud magic-link onboarding already mints a tenant per email
(`src/platform/auth/cloud.ts`). The data model was never the blocker to adding people.
PocketSmith was, because it is a per-user external account: every user would need their
own PocketSmith subscription and their own developer key. That is a referral, not a
product.

The onboarding-model inversion is the heart of this migration:

| | PocketSmith (today) | Basiq (target) |
|---|---|---|
| Secret material | One **per-user** dev key, each user supplies their own | One **app-level** API key, held once by Penny |
| User onboarding | User needs a PocketSmith account + generates a key | User clicks "connect bank", consents under CDR |
| Categorisation | Inherited from the user's PocketSmith category tree | Penny owns it (Basiq enrich + user rules) |
| Bank linking | PocketSmith does it, off-platform | Penny hosts the consent flow, in-app |

Moving to Basiq does not just remove a cost. It removes the only thing standing between
"my budget app" and "a product", and it removes the per-user onboarding friction
entirely. The price is that Penny now owns two things PocketSmith was doing silently:
the bank-linking/consent lifecycle, and categorisation.

## 2. Architecture: blast radius

The good news, confirmed by reading the code: the provider is already isolated in
`src/ingest/`. The envelope engine, budget engine, store, server, and UI consume a
neutral `Tx` shape (`src/platform/store.ts:17`) and never see the provider. The client
docstring states it outright: "the envelope engine never talks to PocketSmith".

**Changes (the swap surface):**

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/ingest/client.ts` | Replaced by a provider behind a new `IngestProvider` port; `BasiqClient` is the new concrete |
| `src/ingest/sync.ts` | Depends on `IngestProvider`, not `PocketSmithClient`; gains job-poll before read |
| `src/ingest/backfill.ts` | Same: provider-typed, pages Basiq transactions |
| `src/ingest/map.ts` | New mapper: Basiq transaction → `Tx` |
| `src/platform/secrets.ts` | New `SecretName` for the app-level Basiq key; `requirePocketSmithKey` retired |
| `src/ingest/` (new) | `provider.ts` (port), `basiq/` (client, consent, jobs, enrich), `categorise.ts` |
| Store schema | New tenant tables: Basiq user/connection/consent state; category rules; category set |
| `src/server/handlers/settings.ts` | New connect-bank / consent flow endpoints |

**Unchanged (the contract that protects everything downstream):** the `Tx` shape, the
`Store` interface, the envelope engine, the budget engine, the effective-dated
category→envelope mapping (ISC-19), the Inbox fallback (ISC-20), the event log, the UI
grid. **`Tx.categoryId` is the single coupling point** between ingest and the rest of the
app. Preserve its meaning (a stable internal category id) and the swap is contained.

## 3. The `IngestProvider` port

Abstracts the provider so `sync`/`backfill` never name a concrete client (ISC-105,
ISC-106). Sketch (TypeScript, illustrative):

```ts
// src/ingest/provider.ts
export interface RawTxnPage {
  readonly txns: readonly unknown[]; // provider-native rows, verbatim (ISC-12)
  readonly nextCursor: string | null;
}

export interface IngestProvider {
  /** Ensure the tenant is linked and data is fresh. Establishes/refreshes the
   *  connection and BLOCKS until the provider's fetch job completes (ISC-113). */
  ensureFresh(userId: UserId): Promise<void>;

  /** Page a tenant's transactions. `since` = inclusive lower postDate bound for
   *  incremental sync (ISC-116); omitted for full backfill from `startDate`. */
  paginate(userId: UserId, q: { startDate?: string; since?: string }):
    AsyncGenerator<RawTxnPage, void, unknown>;

  /** Map one provider-native row to the store Tx shape. categoryId is left null
   *  here; the Categoriser assigns it downstream (ISC-117, ISC-120). */
  toStoreTx(raw: unknown): Tx;

  /** Consent lifecycle surface (Basiq-specific behaviour, port-neutral shape). */
  consentStatus(userId: UserId): Promise<{ ok: boolean; expiresAt: string | null }>;
}
```

`runSync`/`runBackfill` keep their current shape and event-logging; they call
`provider.ensureFresh(userId)` first, then drain `provider.paginate(...)`, then
`toStoreTxs` → `Categoriser` → `store.upsertTransactions`. The PocketSmith pull-only
constraint (ISC-9) survives: Basiq's model is poll-a-job, not a webhook listener
(ISC-119).

## 4. BasiqProvider design

Base URL `https://au-api.basiq.io`. Header `basiq-version` is required on every call.

### 4.1 Auth / server token (ISC-108, ISC-109)

- App API key held in `SecretStore` under a new `SecretName` (`basiq_api_key`),
  resolved at composition root. Never plaintext at rest, in env, git, or logs (ISC-109,
  mirrors ISC-56).
- `POST /token` with `Authorization: Basic <api-key>` and `scope=SERVER_ACCESS` returns a
  short-lived `access_token` (~60 min) **[confirm-in-sandbox]**. Cache it; refresh on
  expiry or on a 401.
- A separate `CLIENT_ACCESS` token, scoped to a single Basiq user, is minted for the
  in-browser Consent UI (§4.3). It never carries server privileges.

### 4.2 Tenant ↔ Basiq user (ISC-110)

- On first connect, `POST /users { email }` → Basiq `userId`. Persist it on the tenant
  (new store column / table, tenant-scoped). This is identity-bearing but not secret, so
  it lives in the `Store`, not the `SecretStore`.

### 4.3 Bank linking via Consent UI (ISC-111)

- Mint a `CLIENT_ACCESS` token for the tenant's Basiq user.
- Redirect the user to the Basiq Consent UI (`https://consent.basiq.io/...?token=...`)
  **[confirm-in-sandbox]**. The user selects their institution (ANZ, NAB, Macquarie) and
  authorises under CDR. **No bank credential ever touches Penny** (ISC-111) — that is the
  whole point of CDR vs screen-scraping.
- On return, a `connection` exists on the Basiq user. Persist `connectionId`,
  institution, and consent `expiresAt` per tenant (ISC-112).

### 4.4 Refresh + job poll (ISC-113)

- Data is fetched asynchronously. `POST /users/{userId}/connections/{id}/refresh` (or the
  connection create) returns a `job` with steps (`retrieve-accounts`,
  `retrieve-transactions`). Poll `GET /jobs/{jobId}` until all steps report `success`
  before reading data **[confirm-in-sandbox]**. `ensureFresh` owns this.

### 4.5 Fetch (ISC-115, ISC-116)

- Backfill: `GET /users/{userId}/transactions` paged via `links.next` to completion
  (ISC-115), from a parameterised start date (reuse the two-year default, ISC-6).
- Incremental: filter `transaction.postDate.gt('YYYY-MM-DD')` against the last successful
  sync bookmark (`getLastSyncAt`, ISC-116). Bookmark advances only on a fully drained run,
  exactly as today.

### 4.6 Mapping Basiq transaction → `Tx` (ISC-117, ISC-118)

Target shape is fixed by `src/platform/store.ts:17`. **[confirm-in-sandbox]** the Basiq
field names and the amount sign convention before passing the ISC.

| `Tx` field | Source | Notes |
|------------|--------|-------|
| `id` | `transaction.id` | string, stable, idempotent upsert key |
| `date` | `transaction.postDate` (fallback `transactionDate`) | ISO date slice |
| `amountCents` | `round(parseFloat(transaction.amount) * 100)` | **signed, negative = outflow** (ISC-118). Basiq amount is a signed string; assert against `direction` (`debit`/`credit`) |
| `accountId` | `transaction.account` | Basiq account id |
| `categoryId` | **null at map time** | assigned by the Categoriser (§5) |
| `envelopeId` | `null` | envelope engine resolves at read time, unchanged |
| `payee` | `enrich.merchant.businessName` ?? `description` | merchant when enriched, else raw description |
| `isTransfer` | `class === 'transfer'` | maps to the existing transfer-exclusion rule (ISC-22) |
| `isPending` | `status === 'pending'` | preserves ISC-23 |
| `rawJson` | `JSON.stringify(transaction)` | verbatim Basiq row (ISC-12 preserved) |

The money invariant from the current mapper holds unchanged: decimal → integer cents,
rounded once, sign preserved.

## 5. The categorisation layer (the real work)

PocketSmith handed Penny transactions already filed into the user's own category tree,
and Penny's entire envelope assignment keys on that category id (`map.ts` set
`categoryId = raw.category?.id`; ISC-19 maps category→envelope; ISC-86 maps tx→envelope by
category). **Basiq has no per-user category tree.** It provides its own enrichment
taxonomy (merchant, `class`, ANZSIC division/subdivision), which does not match
PocketSmith ids and is not user-owned.

For a product this is non-optional anyway: you cannot require each user to arrive with
pre-categorised data. So Penny must own categorisation. The design keeps the blast radius
tiny by **synthesising a stable internal `categoryId`** so the existing mapping model is
untouched (ISC-124).

### 5.1 The Categoriser (ISC-120, ISC-121)

A pure function over a transaction, producing an internal `categoryId`:

1. **Enrich default.** Derive a starting category from Basiq enrich (merchant + `class` +
   ANZSIC), mapped through a Penny-owned static lookup into Penny's internal category set.
2. **User rules override.** Apply the tenant's editable rules; a matching rule wins over
   the enrich default (ISC-121).
3. **Fallback.** No match → the "uncategorised" internal category, which the existing
   effective-dated mapping resolves to the Inbox envelope (ISC-123, preserving ISC-19/20).

### 5.2 Category rules (ISC-122)

A tenant-scoped, effective-dated rule: `payee/merchant pattern → internal categoryId`.
Effective-dating matches the existing mapping model so re-categorising history is
deterministic. Rules are user-editable in the UI (a later UI ISC; the engine and store
land first).

### 5.3 What stays unchanged (ISC-124)

The envelope engine, the effective-dated category→envelope mapping (ISC-19), the Inbox
fallback (ISC-20), and the grid do not change. `categoryId` is the only coupling point;
the Categoriser is responsible for filling it, replacing the line in the old mapper.

### 5.4 Non-destructive re-run (ISC-125)

Re-running the categoriser refreshes the enrich-derived default but never overwrites a
user's explicit category override or their rules, mirroring the ISC-17 base-vs-overlay
discipline already used for transactions.

### 5.5 Seeding and historical migration (ISC-127)

- The envelope tree is already seeded from Nick's spreadsheet, not the PocketSmith tree
  (ISC-96), so envelope seeding is unaffected.
- The category→envelope **mapping** needs a new category source. A one-time migration maps
  the existing PocketSmith-categorised transactions onto Penny's internal category set so
  historical envelope balances are preserved across the cutover (ISC-127). The PocketSmith
  category id on each historical `rawJson` is the bridge for that one-time map.

## 6. Consent & CDR compliance posture

- **Single-user now (Nick only):** lightest path. Penny holds the Basiq app key; Nick
  consents to ANZ/NAB/Macquarie via the Consent UI. Basiq holds the CDR accreditation;
  Penny consumes it.
- **Multi-user later (the product):** serving other people's banking data under CDR is a
  heavier posture even with Basiq accredited. Penny would operate under Basiq's
  representative/consent model with consent dashboards, data-minimisation, and deletion
  obligations. This is the cost that *replaces* the per-user PocketSmith subscription cost.
  **Deferred** until Penny is actually opened to others; the architecture is built
  product-shaped now so flipping it on is onboarding + compliance, not a re-architecture.
- **CDR consent expiry (ISC-114):** consents expire (up to 12 months). Detect expiry,
  surface a re-consent prompt before data goes stale, and never report an empty post-expiry
  sync as success.

## 7. Secrets / identity model change

| Concern | Today | Target |
|---------|-------|--------|
| `SecretStore` holds | per-user `pocketsmith_developer_key` | app-level `basiq_api_key` (one) |
| Per-tenant in `Store` | (nothing provider-specific) | Basiq `userId`, `connectionId`, consent `expiresAt` |
| Onboarding input | email + user's PocketSmith dev key | email + in-app bank consent (ISC-128) |

ISC-3 ("dev key resolved through the SecretStore for the authenticated user") is
superseded: the secret is now app-level, and the per-user material is consent state in the
`Store`, not a key. ISC-54/55 (per-user dev key, local + cloud KMS) are re-pointed at the
app-level Basiq key. ISC-56 (never plaintext) carries over verbatim to the Basiq key.

## 8. Migration & decommission sequence

1. Land the `IngestProvider` port; make `sync`/`backfill` provider-typed (ISC-105, ISC-106).
2. Build `BasiqProvider`: token, user, consent, job-poll, fetch, mapper (ISC-107..ISC-118).
3. Build the Categoriser + rules + internal category set (ISC-120..ISC-125).
4. Backfill Nick's own data via Basiq; verify parity against the existing PocketSmith data
   (transaction counts, balances) before cutover.
5. One-time historical category migration (ISC-127).
6. Remove PocketSmith from the runtime path once parity is verified (ISC-126); keep the
   pinned OpenAPI artefact in git history only.
7. Confirm no per-user dev key is needed to onboard (ISC-128).

## 9. Confirm-in-sandbox checklist (BUILD gate)

These are design assumptions from Basiq's documented model that must be verified against
the live sandbox before the matching ISC passes. Do not mark them `[x]` on intent:

- Token endpoint scopes (`SERVER_ACCESS` / `CLIENT_ACCESS`) and TTLs.
- Consent UI URL, token handoff, and return/callback contract.
- Job step names and the terminal success signal.
- Transaction field names: `postDate`/`transactionDate`, `amount` sign, `direction`,
  `class` values, `status` enum, `enrich.merchant`/`enrich.category` shape.
- Transactions pagination cursor (`links.next`) and the postDate filter syntax.
- Institution coverage and CDR data scopes for ANZ, NAB, Macquarie.
- Commercial: dev/sandbox is free; production access plan, per-connection pricing, and
  whether a single-user (then multi-user) use case is accepted.

## 10. ISC index

Provider abstraction: ISC-105, ISC-106, ISC-107.
Auth/token: ISC-108, ISC-109.
User/connection/consent lifecycle: ISC-110, ISC-111, ISC-112, ISC-113, ISC-114.
Fetch + mapping: ISC-115, ISC-116, ISC-117, ISC-118, ISC-119.
Categorisation: ISC-120, ISC-121, ISC-122, ISC-123, ISC-124, ISC-125.
Migration/decommission: ISC-126, ISC-127, ISC-128.

```ts
export interface IngestProvider {
  /** Ensure the tenant is linked and data is fresh. Establishes/refreshes the
   *  connection and BLOCKS until the provider's fetch job completes (ISC-113). */
  ensureFresh(userId: UserId): Promise<void>;

  /** Page a tenant's transactions. `since` = inclusive lower postDate bound for
   *  incremental sync (ISC-116); omitted for full backfill from `startDate`. */
  paginate(userId: UserId, q: { startDate?: string; since?: string }):
    AsyncGenerator<RawTxnPage, void, unknown>;

  /** Map one provider-native row to the store Tx shape. categoryId is left null
   *  here; the Categoriser assigns it downstream (ISC-117, ISC-120). */
  toStoreTx(raw: unknown): Tx;

  /** Consent lifecycle surface (Basiq-specific behaviour, port-neutral shape). */
  consentStatus(userId: UserId): Promise<{ ok: boolean; expiresAt: string | null }>;
}
```

`runSync`/`runBackfill` keep their current shape and event-logging; they call
`provider.ensureFresh(userId)` first, then drain `provider.paginate(...)`, then
`toStoreTxs` → `Categoriser` → `store.upsertTransactions`. The PocketSmith pull-only
constraint (ISC-9) survives: Basiq's model is poll-a-job, not a webhook listener
(ISC-119).

## 4. BasiqProvider design

Base URL `https://au-api.basiq.io`. Header `basiq-version` is required on every call.

### 4.1 Auth / server token (ISC-108, ISC-109)

- App API key held in `SecretStore` under a new `SecretName` (`basiq_api_key`),
  resolved at composition root. Never plaintext at rest, in env, git, or logs (ISC-109,
  mirrors ISC-56).
- `POST /token` with `Authorization: Basic <api-key>` and `scope=SERVER_ACCESS` returns a
  short-lived `access_token` (~60 min) **[confirm-in-sandbox]**. Cache it; refresh on
  expiry or on a 401.
- A separate `CLIENT_ACCESS` token, scoped to a single Basiq user, is minted for the
  in-browser Consent UI (§4.3). It never carries server privileges.

### 4.2 Tenant ↔ Basiq user (ISC-110)

- On first connect, `POST /users { email }` → Basiq `userId`. Persist it on the tenant
  (new store column / table, tenant-scoped). This is identity-bearing but not secret, so
  it lives in the `Store`, not the `SecretStore`.

### 4.3 Bank linking via Consent UI (ISC-111)

- Mint a `CLIENT_ACCESS` token for the tenant's Basiq user.
- Redirect the user to the Basiq Consent UI (`https://consent.basiq.io/...?token=...`)
  **[confirm-in-sandbox]**. The user selects their institution (ANZ, NAB, Macquarie) and
  authorises under CDR. **No bank credential ever touches Penny** (ISC-111) — that is the
  whole point of CDR vs screen-scraping.
- On return, a `connection` exists on the Basiq user. Persist `connectionId`,
  institution, and consent `expiresAt` per tenant (ISC-112).

### 4.4 Refresh + job poll (ISC-113)

- Data is fetched asynchronously. `POST /users/{userId}/connections/{id}/refresh` (or the
  connection create) returns a `job` with steps (`retrieve-accounts`,
  `retrieve-transactions`). Poll `GET /jobs/{jobId}` until all steps report `success`
  before reading data **[confirm-in-sandbox]**. `ensureFresh` owns this.

### 4.5 Fetch (ISC-115, ISC-116)

- Backfill: `GET /users/{userId}/transactions` paged via `links.next` to completion
  (ISC-115), from a parameterised start date (reuse the two-year default, ISC-6).
- Incremental: filter `transaction.postDate.gt('YYYY-MM-DD')` against the last successful
  sync bookmark (`getLastSyncAt`, ISC-116). Bookmark advances only on a fully drained run,
  exactly as today.

### 4.6 Mapping Basiq transaction → `Tx` (ISC-117, ISC-118)

Target shape is fixed by `src/platform/store.ts:17`. **[confirm-in-sandbox]** the Basiq
field names and the amount sign convention before passing the ISC.

| `Tx` field | Source | Notes |
|------------|--------|-------|
| `id` | `transaction.id` | string, stable, idempotent upsert key |
| `date` | `transaction.postDate` (fallback `transactionDate`) | ISO date slice |
| `amountCents` | `round(parseFloat(transaction.amount) * 100)` | **signed, negative = outflow** (ISC-118). Basiq amount is a signed string; assert against `direction` (`debit`/`credit`) |
| `accountId` | `transaction.account` | Basiq account id |
| `categoryId` | **null at map time** | assigned by the Categoriser (§5) |
| `envelopeId` | `null` | envelope engine resolves at read time, unchanged |
| `payee` | `enrich.merchant.businessName` ?? `description` | merchant when enriched, else raw description |
| `isTransfer` | `class === 'transfer'` | maps to the existing transfer-exclusion rule (ISC-22) |
| `isPending` | `status === 'pending'` | preserves ISC-23 |
| `rawJson` | `JSON.stringify(transaction)` | verbatim Basiq row (ISC-12 preserved) |

The money invariant from the current mapper holds unchanged: decimal → integer cents,
rounded once, sign preserved.

## 5. The categorisation layer (the real work)

PocketSmith handed Penny transactions already filed into the user's own category tree,
and Penny's entire envelope assignment keys on that category id (`map.ts` set
`categoryId = raw.category?.id`; ISC-19 maps category→envelope; ISC-86 maps tx→envelope by
category). **Basiq has no per-user category tree.** It provides its own enrichment
taxonomy (merchant, `class`, ANZSIC division/subdivision), which does not match
PocketSmith ids and is not user-owned.

For a product this is non-optional anyway: you cannot require each user to arrive with
pre-categorised data. So Penny must own categorisation. The design keeps the blast radius
tiny by **synthesising a stable internal `categoryId`** so the existing mapping model is
untouched (ISC-124).

### 5.1 The Categoriser (ISC-120, ISC-121)

A pure function over a transaction, producing an internal `categoryId`:

1. **Enrich default.** Derive a starting category from Basiq enrich (merchant + `class` +
   ANZSIC), mapped through a Penny-owned static lookup into Penny's internal category set.
2. **User rules override.** Apply the tenant's editable rules; a matching rule wins over
   the enrich default (ISC-121).
3. **Fallback.** No match → the "uncategorised" internal category, which the existing
   effective-dated mapping resolves to the Inbox envelope (ISC-123, preserving ISC-19/20).

### 5.2 Category rules (ISC-122)

A tenant-scoped, effective-dated rule: `payee/merchant pattern → internal categoryId`.
Effective-dating matches the existing mapping model so re-categorising history is
deterministic. Rules are user-editable in the UI (a later UI ISC; the engine and store
land first).

### 5.3 What stays unchanged (ISC-124)

The envelope engine, the effective-dated category→envelope mapping (ISC-19), the Inbox
fallback (ISC-20), and the grid do not change. `categoryId` is the only coupling point;
the Categoriser is responsible for filling it, replacing the line in the old mapper.

### 5.4 Non-destructive re-run (ISC-125)

Re-running the categoriser refreshes the enrich-derived default but never overwrites a
user's explicit category override or their rules, mirroring the ISC-17 base-vs-overlay
discipline already used for transactions.

### 5.5 Seeding and historical migration (ISC-127)

- The envelope tree is already seeded from Nick's spreadsheet, not the PocketSmith tree
  (ISC-96), so envelope seeding is unaffected.
- The category→envelope **mapping** needs a new category source. A one-time migration maps
  the existing PocketSmith-categorised transactions onto Penny's internal category set so
  historical envelope balances are preserved across the cutover (ISC-127). The PocketSmith
  category id on each historical `rawJson` is the bridge for that one-time map.

## 6. Consent & CDR compliance posture

- **Single-user now (Nick only):** lightest path. Penny holds the Basiq app key; Nick
  consents to ANZ/NAB/Macquarie via the Consent UI. Basiq holds the CDR accreditation;
  Penny consumes it.
- **Multi-user later (the product):** serving other people's banking data under CDR is a
  heavier posture even with Basiq accredited. Penny would operate under Basiq's
  representative/consent model with consent dashboards, data-minimisation, and deletion
  obligations. This is the cost that *replaces* the per-user PocketSmith subscription cost.
  **Deferred** until Penny is actually opened to others; the architecture is built
  product-shaped now so flipping it on is onboarding + compliance, not a re-architecture.
- **CDR consent expiry (ISC-114):** consents expire (up to 12 months). Detect expiry,
  surface a re-consent prompt before data goes stale, and never report an empty post-expiry
  sync as success.

## 7. Secrets / identity model change

| Concern | Today | Target |
|---------|-------|--------|
| `SecretStore` holds | per-user `pocketsmith_developer_key` | app-level `basiq_api_key` (one) |
| Per-tenant in `Store` | (nothing provider-specific) | Basiq `userId`, `connectionId`, consent `expiresAt` |
| Onboarding input | email + user's PocketSmith dev key | email + in-app bank consent (ISC-128) |

ISC-3 ("dev key resolved through the SecretStore for the authenticated user") is
superseded: the secret is now app-level, and the per-user material is consent state in the
`Store`, not a key. ISC-54/55 (per-user dev key, local + cloud KMS) are re-pointed at the
app-level Basiq key. ISC-56 (never plaintext) carries over verbatim to the Basiq key.

## 8. Migration & decommission sequence

1. Land the `IngestProvider` port; make `sync`/`backfill` provider-typed (ISC-105, ISC-106).
2. Build `BasiqProvider`: token, user, consent, job-poll, fetch, mapper (ISC-107..ISC-118).
3. Build the Categoriser + rules + internal category set (ISC-120..ISC-125).
4. Backfill Nick's own data via Basiq; verify parity against the existing PocketSmith data
   (transaction counts, balances) before cutover.
5. One-time historical category migration (ISC-127).
6. Remove PocketSmith from the runtime path once parity is verified (ISC-126); keep the
   pinned OpenAPI artefact in git history only.
7. Confirm no per-user dev key is needed to onboard (ISC-128).

## 9. Confirm-in-sandbox checklist (BUILD gate)

These are design assumptions from Basiq's documented model that must be verified against
the live sandbox before the matching ISC passes. Do not mark them `[x]` on intent:

- Token endpoint scopes (`SERVER_ACCESS` / `CLIENT_ACCESS`) and TTLs.
- Consent UI URL, token handoff, and return/callback contract.
- Job step names and the terminal success signal.
- Transaction field names: `postDate`/`transactionDate`, `amount` sign, `direction`,
  `class` values, `status` enum, `enrich.merchant`/`enrich.category` shape.
- Transactions pagination cursor (`links.next`) and the postDate filter syntax.
- Institution coverage and CDR data scopes for ANZ, NAB, Macquarie.
- Commercial: dev/sandbox is free; production access plan, per-connection pricing, and
  whether a single-user (then multi-user) use case is accepted.

## 10. ISC index

Provider abstraction: ISC-105, ISC-106, ISC-107.
Auth/token: ISC-108, ISC-109.
User/connection/consent lifecycle: ISC-110, ISC-111, ISC-112, ISC-113, ISC-114.
Fetch + mapping: ISC-115, ISC-116, ISC-117, ISC-118, ISC-119.
Categorisation: ISC-120, ISC-121, ISC-122, ISC-123, ISC-124, ISC-125.
Migration/decommission: ISC-126, ISC-127, ISC-128.

- [ ] ISC-106: Anti: No ingest module (sync, backfill) imports a provider-concrete client type directly

- [ ] ISC-108: The Basiq server token is obtained via POST /token with the app API key, cached to expiry, and refreshed on 401
- [ ] ISC-109: Anti: The Basiq app API key never appears as plaintext at rest, in env files, git, or logs
- [ ] ISC-110: A Basiq user is created per tenant and the Basiq userId persisted in the tenant-scoped Store
- [ ] ISC-111: A bank connection is established via the Basiq Consent UI; Anti: no bank credential ever reaches Penny
- [ ] ISC-112: Connection state (connectionId, institution, consent expiresAt) is persisted per tenant
- [ ] ISC-113: A connection refresh issues a job and polls GET /jobs/{id} to terminal success before any data read
- [ ] ISC-114: Anti: An expired CDR consent surfaces a re-consent prompt and is never reported as a successful empty sync
- [ ] ISC-115: Backfill pages the Basiq transactions endpoint to completion via links.next
- [ ] ISC-116: Incremental sync filters Basiq transactions by postDate greater than the last successful run bookmark
- [ ] ISC-117: A Basiq transaction maps to the store Tx shape (signed amount to cents, postDate to date, status to isPending, class transfer to isTransfer, merchant to payee, verbatim JSON to rawJson)
- [ ] ISC-118: Anti: The mapper preserves negative=outflow; a debit never lands as a positive amount
- [ ] ISC-119: Anti: No webhook or push listener for Basiq events exists; sync stays pull-poll only (preserves ISC-9 for the new provider)
- [ ] ISC-120: A Categoriser assigns every ingested transaction a stable internal categoryId from Penny's own category set, independent of any provider taxonomy
- [ ] ISC-121: The Categoriser derives a default category from Basiq enrich, then lets a matching user rule override it
- [ ] ISC-122: A user-editable category rule maps a payee/merchant pattern to an internal categoryId; rules are tenant-scoped and effective-dated
- [ ] ISC-123: An uncategorised transaction resolves to the Inbox envelope via the existing effective-dated category-to-envelope mapping (preserves ISC-19, ISC-20)
- [ ] ISC-124: Anti: The envelope engine and the category-to-envelope mapping are unchanged by the swap; Tx.categoryId stays the only coupling point
- [ ] ISC-125: Anti: Re-running the Categoriser never overwrites a user's explicit category override or rules (mirrors ISC-17)
- [ ] ISC-126: PocketSmith ingest (client, /me, X-Developer-Key) is removed from the runtime path once Basiq backfill verifies data parity on Nick's own data
- [ ] ISC-127: A one-time migration maps existing PocketSmith-categorised transactions onto the internal category set so historical envelope balances are preserved

- 2026-06-26 00:00: show-your-math (delegation floor): the ingest-spine implementation is delegated to one engineering agent against this ISA; the platform-seams skeleton and schema are authored by the primary because they are the architecturally load-bearing surface where the cloud-ready contract must be exact. Council/RedTeam delegation was not selected; the design space here is already resolved by the existing architect review, so adversarial idea-generation would add noise rather than signal.
- 2026-06-29: PROVIDER PIVOT to direct Australian bank feeds via Basiq (CDR), off PocketSmith. Nick's drivers: drop the dependency, kill the PocketSmith cost, and stop building on a bridge if Penny may serve other people later. Decisive fact: Penny is already multi-tenant (Store scoped by userId, ISC-47/48; cloud magic-link onboarding), so PocketSmith was the only per-user external blocker to a product. Resolution: abstract the provider behind an `IngestProvider` port, implement `BasiqProvider`, and have Penny own categorisation (Basiq enrich + user rules) since a product cannot inherit each user's pre-categorised tree. Build single-user now (Nick only), product-shaped; defer multi-user CDR-representative onboarding. Full design in docs/BASIQ_MIGRATION_SPEC.md. Supersedes ISC-1, ISC-2, ISC-3, ISC-84 (category source), ISC-86; adds ISC-105..ISC-128.
- 2026-06-29: SECRET MODEL INVERTED. PocketSmith required a per-user developer key in the SecretStore; Basiq uses one app-level API key plus per-user in-app CDR consent. ISC-3 superseded; ISC-54/55 re-pointed at the app-level Basiq key; ISC-56 carries over to it. Per-user material (Basiq userId, connectionId, consent expiry) lives in the Store, not the SecretStore. This removes user onboarding friction entirely (ISC-128) and is why Basiq enables the product where PocketSmith could not.
- 2026-06-29: SCOPE. This task delivered the ISA extension plus the design spec only (Nick approved "scaffold the ISA + spec the provider"). No production code written; BUILD of the provider and Categoriser is the next gated step. Basiq API field names and sign conventions are marked confirm-in-sandbox in the spec and MUST be verified against the live Basiq sandbox before the matching ISCs (ISC-108, 111, 113, 115, 116, 117, 118) pass.

14	# BudgetBuddy (envelope-os) — Project ISA
15	
16	> Surface name **BudgetBuddy**. Codebase folder `envelope-os`. Zero-based envelope budgeting layer on direct Australian bank feeds (Basiq / CDR, migrating off PocketSmith), feeding PAI Pulse. AUD, personal-finance-grade security. **Local-first now, cloud-ready by construction.** One codebase ships to two deployment targets — Local (Tailscale, single principal at runtime) and Cloud (public at `nicholaswood.com.au/budget`, multi-tenant) — and the only difference between them is configuration plus two swapped adapters, never the data model or the business logic.
17	
18	## Problem
19	
20	PocketSmith owns Nick's bank feeds and categorisation across ANZ (primary), NAB (credit card), and Macquarie, but its envelope handling is weak and it does not implement zero-based envelope budgeting. Dave Ramsey's EveryDollar and similar apps do implement the methodology but cannot connect to Australian banks. The result is that Nick runs envelope budgeting in his head on top of PocketSmith, which does not scale, does not survive a credit-card statement cycle cleanly, and gives no trustworthy single number for "where am I against budget right now". There is no time-travel view of envelope balances at a past date, no enforced every-dollar-allocated discipline, and no surface that feeds the state into Pulse. Secondly, the original build was scoped local-only and single-user; if it works, Nick wants the option to let another person use it by handing over only their email and their own PocketSmith developer key, which a local-only, single-tenant design cannot do without a painful retrofit.
21	
22	## Vision
23	
24	Nick opens Pulse and sees one honest line. Unallocated dollars, the worst three overspends, and whether the credit-card holding balance still matches NAB. He opens BudgetBuddy on his phone — installed as a PWA, reached over Tailscale. He never plans a month; the budget is the recurring template and it simply rolls into each new month on its own. When something changes he adjusts one envelope or moves money, the change is remembered going forward, and it lands in a budget history he can scroll back through. When a late transaction lands weeks later, the envelope it belongs to moves on the day it was spent, not when the statement closes, so the budget never lies about the past. The euphoric surprise is twofold: the holding-versus-NAB tripwire — a single number that, when it drifts, tells Nick something is wrong before he would otherwise have noticed — and the realisation that the day he decides to let someone else use BudgetBuddy, it is already a per-user multi-tenant app; he adds them with an email and their dev key, flips one config value, deploys to GCP, and nothing in the ledger, the envelope engine, or the UI had to change.
25	
26	## Out of Scope
27	
28	The MVP does not split one category across multiple envelopes. Mapping stays many categories to one envelope. A dedicated sinking-fund target type is not built. Annual envelopes are treated as monthly target divided by twelve for the MVP. There is no mobile quick-add of purchases and no offline transaction capture — the PWA is read-and-allocate over Tailscale, not an offline write queue. There is no auto-allocation engine and no agent-proposed allocations. There is no reporting suite beyond what the grid and detail pages show, no PDF or CSV export, and no what-if replay queries against the event log. There is no multi-currency support. There is no joint-finance surface; the data model is multi-tenant per-user, not joint-account shared-ledger. **Cloud hosting is built-ready, not deployed.** The cloud adapters (email magic-link auth, KMS-encrypted per-user secrets, Postgres data layer) are written and unit-tested behind their interfaces so the switch is config-only, but standing up the public GCP service, registering the `/budget` route on `nicholaswood.com.au`, and onboarding a second human are deliberate later steps, not MVP deliverables. Direct bank-CSV reconciliation against PocketSmith feeds is a later trust layer, not MVP.
29	
30	## Principles
31	
32	- The envelope is the user-facing primitive. PocketSmith categories are inputs. Envelopes are how Nick thinks and decides.
33	- Cash-basis fidelity to the envelope metaphor. A swipe decrements the envelope on the day it happens, regardless of which card moved.
34	- Every dollar is conserved. A forgiven overspend is not free money. The deficit is always booked somewhere, never silently leaked.
35	- Local-first. Personal financial data does not leave the owner's machine without a deliberate, per-action choice. In local mode there is no cloud egress of transactions at all.
36	- **Cloud-ready by construction, not by rewrite.** The data model is multi-tenant from the first migration; every piece of identity-bearing state carries a `user_id`. Deployment differences (who authenticates, where secrets live, which database backs the store) sit behind interfaces. Business logic never knows or branches on which deployment target it is running in.
37	- **One tenant per principal.** Each user owns their own PocketSmith developer key, their own transactions, their own envelopes and budget. There is no shared data between tenants. Onboarding a person is: their email plus their PocketSmith dev key.
38	- The event log is the source of truth and the audit log. Future-Nick can always ask why an envelope went negative on a given day and get an answer.
39	- The thing is the source of truth, not the task. This ISA at the project root is iterated continuously, not recreated per task.
40	
41	## Constraints
42	
43	- bun plus TypeScript only. No Python. No npm or npx. Australian English. AUD only. No em dashes in prose.
44	- **Single codebase, two deployment targets, one switch.** A `DEPLOY_MODE` value of `local` or `cloud` is the only thing that selects deployment behaviour. No business module reads `DEPLOY_MODE`; only the composition root (dependency wiring) does.
45	- **Multi-tenant schema from the first migration.** A `users` table exists. Every tenant-scoped table carries a non-null `user_id` foreign key to `users.id`. Local mode seeds exactly one user (Nick) and runs single-tenant at runtime over a multi-tenant schema. There is no separate single-tenant schema that later needs migrating.
46	- **Auth sits behind an `AuthProvider` interface.** Local implementation: Tailscale device trust plus a PIN held in the secret store, thirty-minute idle session. Cloud implementation: passwordless email magic-link sign-in (request link, verify token, mint httpOnly+Secure+SameSite session cookie). No route handler or business module depends on which implementation is active; they depend only on the resolved authenticated `user_id`.
47	- **Secrets sit behind a `SecretStore` interface, keyed per user.** Each user's PocketSmith `X-Developer-Key` is fetched through the store for the authenticated `user_id` at request time. Local implementation: the PAI secrets store / OS keychain / an encrypted local file. Cloud implementation: envelope encryption via GCP KMS with ciphertext stored in the database. A developer key never appears in env files, git, logs, or as plaintext at rest.
48	- **Data access sits behind a thin store layer; SQL stays Postgres-portable.** Local persistence is SQLite via `bun:sqlite`, single file, single writer owned by one Bun process. No business module imports `bun:sqlite` directly — they depend on the store interface. Business queries avoid SQLite-only syntax so the Postgres adapter (cloud) is a drop-in. The cloud Postgres adapter is written and unit-tested but not the local default.

Nick's drivers: drop the dependency, kill the PocketSmith cost, and stop building on a bridge if BudgetBuddy may serve other people later. Decisive fact: BudgetBuddy is already multi-tenant (Store scoped by userId, ISC-47/48; cloud magic-link onboarding), so PocketSmith was the only per-user external blocker to a product. Resolution: abstract the provider behind an `IngestProvider` port, implement `BasiqProvider`, and have BudgetBuddy own categorisation (Basiq enrich + user rules) since a product cannot inherit each user's pre-categorised tree. Build single-user now (Nick only), product-shaped; defer multi-user CDR-representative onboarding. Full design in docs/BASIQ_MIGRATION_SPEC.md. Supersedes ISC-1, ISC-2, ISC-3, ISC-84 (category source), ISC-86; adds ISC-105..ISC-128.

- 2026-06-29: SECRET MODEL INVERTED. PocketSmith required a per-user developer key in the SecretStore; Basiq uses one app-level API key plus per-user in-app CDR consent. ISC-3 superseded; ISC-54/55 re-pointed at the app-level Basiq key; ISC-56 carries over to it. Per-user material (Basiq userId, connectionId, consent expiry) lives in the Store, not the SecretStore. This removes user onboarding friction entirely (ISC-128) and is why Basiq enables the product where PocketSmith could not.

- 2026-06-29: SCOPE. This task delivered the ISA extension plus the design spec only (Nick approved "scaffold the ISA + spec the provider"). No production code written; BUILD of the provider and Categoriser is the next gated step. Basiq API field names and sign conventions are marked confirm-in-sandbox in the spec and MUST be verified against the live Basiq sandbox before the matching ISCs (ISC-108, 111, 113, 115, 116, 117, 118) pass.

+- 2026-06-29: EXTERNAL PREREQUISITE (BUILD gate, owner: Nick). Starting the Basiq build requires a free Basiq developer account to obtain sandbox API keys (dashboard.basiq.io).
